utterances.text: Well, I think you just said to the Presiding Judge that the remarks that you made about Mr. Karadzic being a good person and a man who was good to his neighbours, you actually restricted that to the time that you were talking about before the war and after the war, didn't you, just a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MILAN PEJIC
utterances.text: -- I gave this statement of mine -- may I say --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Dr. Pejic, can I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think that she has to allow the witness to give an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's hear him out. Yes, Dr. Pejic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel very unpleasant, very embarrassed, when the lady interrupts me in mid-sentence because then my response loses any kind of context. I gave this statement about the period while Dr. Karadzic worked at the Kosevo hospital. That was my understanding of it. It is quite understandable, Your Honours and Madam, that the other side certainly portrayed a different kind of picture regarding Dr. Karadzic. As for my image of Dr. Karadzic, I obtained it before the war indirectly. I first met him in January 1995. Is it clear now? I hope that I've clarified the matter now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I would just like to thank Dr. Pejic for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for your readiness to hear me out. And I'm sorry that I had been interrupted halfway as I wanted to explain some things that happened on the ground and that were important for the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, when the witness answers beyond the scope of the question, sometimes we advise the witness to concentrate on answering the question, but we understand your frustration. But in any event, that concludes your evidence, Dr. Pejic, and on behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just need a moment to change places, Ms. McKenna and I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next witness is Mr. Lubura?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, Goran Sikiras.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sikiras, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, just while we're waiting for the witness to come in, I'd just like to introduce myself to Your Honours. My name is Bronagh McKenna and I'm pleased to appear before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Welcome, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that due to logistical problem we need to adjourn for 15 minutes. We'll resume at five to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sikiras. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sikiras.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D6803 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sikiras, did you provide a statement to the Defence team and can you see it before you on the screen here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I need to ask you the following and it is a reminder for me as well. We need to pause so as to assist the interpreters and have an accurate transcript. Does the statement accurately reflect your words?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Perhaps a name or two is misspelled or omitted. I see one, for example, instead of an A there is an U in item 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Line 5, the third word, the second letter. Instead of O there is U.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the rest, are there any other typographical mistakes and is the content accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign this statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions today that were put to you by the team, would your answers be the same in essence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I seek to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you're not tendering any associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted as next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D06803 receives number D2540, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to read out in the English language a summary of Professor Sikiras's statement. [In English] Goran Sikiras was a school professor. He lived in Vogosca municipality. As soon as the conflict broke out in Sarajevo, barricades were set up and divisions were made based exclusively on the ethnic principle. His village, Grahoviste, was a mono-ethnic Serbian village and the closest was Kobilja Glava, a mono-ethnic Muslim village. The Muslims set up a barricade on the regional road to Vogosca immediately after the referendum about independence. When Goran Sikiras passed the barricade, he was checked and there were seven or eight armed Muslims present. The inhabitants of Grahoviste feared the Muslims because of the barricade and the fact that the Muslims were armed. By March 1992 there were barricades in all the settlements around Sarajevo and in Sarajevo itself, which made it particularly impossible for both teachers and students to go to school and he stopped going to work in April. Out of pure fear for their lives and those of their families, Serbs organised guards in the village of Grahoviste from April until May 1992. Guard was kept around Grahoviste with people carrying hunting rifles and a few automatic rifles owned by members of the reserve police. On 2nd or 3rd of May, 1992, the Muslims began shelling the village of Grahoviste indiscriminately, using mortars from their positions in a playground of the school in Kobilja Glava. The Muslims also fired on the Vogosca municipality, the Pretis factory, Blagovac village, and Hotonj village, Serb part of it. The population of these was exclusively Serbian and many houses and buildings were damaged, and civilians were killed and wounded. The members of the village were terrified and most fled to the surrounding woods. Following the shelling, a search of the surrounding area of the village was conducted on 4th of May, 1992, by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. On May the 12th of 1992, Goran Sikiras and nine other men from his village joined the Bosnian Serb army in the Vogosca platoon and were deployed to Zuc. Zuc and the villages on it were 100 per cent Serbian, and on June 1992, Muslims launched a general attack on this area. [Interpretation] This was the short summary. At this point in time I have no questions of Mr. Sikiras.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Sikiras, as you have noted that your evidence in chief was admitted in written form in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Sikiras.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We met yesterday and, as we discussed, we are limited in time today, so I'd like you to listen carefully to my questions and please answer them as precisely and as concisely as possible. When we spoke yesterday, we discussed a couple of clarifications in respect of your statement. At paragraph 70 of your -- excuse me, at paragraph 20 of your statement, you stated that on the 5th of May, 1992, ten of the men from your village went into the woods on Zuc hill. Yesterday you clarified that you remained in the woods on Zuc, protecting the front line, until the attack of 8th June 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: It is correct, although the number of people who were there could not protect the entire area. We only monitored the village since some ten residents stayed behind and we didn't want any harm to come to them. As for any front lines, it was impossible to establish any with that small number of people we had. I have tried to explain to you the size of the area further afield following the village and the Zuc peak. There was no significant defence to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Again, I'd like you to answer as concisely as possible, if you can listen to the question and simply answer the questions that you were asked.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I'll try my best.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So you stated that during that period your unit was small and disorganised, but it subsequently became part of the Vogosca Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then after the attack of the 8th of June, you moved away from Zuc to another area but remained within the Vogosca Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then in May 1993, you left the Vogosca Brigade to organise a school in Vogosca; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At paragraph 6 of your statement you discuss the barricades set up in March 1992 by the Muslims from Kobilja Glava. And at paragraph 7 you state, with reference to those barricades: "It never occurred to us Serbs to do it." Yesterday you clarified that by "us Serbs" you meant the population of Grahoviste village; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 8 of your statement, you referred to the barricades set up in Sarajevo and in all the settlements around Sarajevo in March.

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: That was the information we had. That was something we heard in the media. We could see reporting to that effect on TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sikiras, many of the barricades in the city of Sarajevo were set up by Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: That is possible. I didn't see any, given the fact that I didn't leave the village area for two months. If I did see anything, I could only see it on TV if it was shown.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, many of the barricades in the Vogosca municipality were set up by Serbs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: That is possible too. I repeat: Throughout the month of April and May up until the 8th of June I was in the forest at Zuc. I didn't go down once until the attack on the 8th of June, and then I was transferred to another location.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, Mr. Sikiras, is it your evidence that you do not know whether any barricades were set up by Serbs in the Vogosca municipality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I suppose there were some, but I didn't see any. It seems to be established that there were barricades. Now, who posted some and where and whether it was the Muslims or Serbs, I already shared what I know in the statement. I guess that was standard practice at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, those barricades that were set up by Serbs were organised by the Serb municipality authorities, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I can't say anything precisely, although it may have been possible. As for what I know, people usually organised themselves. Where there were more families of the same ethnicity, people organised themselves to prevent any surprises. People stood guard around their houses. I mentioned yesterday that I saw the end of the war at a location which I had left in 1993, where people stood guard in front of their houses throughout the war within a perimeter of literally a couple dozen metres. Perhaps you remember it mention -- me mentioning that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At this stage I'd like to call up 65 ter number 45111C, which is a video. The Trial Chamber has already admitted a portion of this video which is a Serbian television interview from 1994. A portion has already been admitted as P968. I'd like to play this video which is just under two minutes long and ask the translation booths to translate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could just pause before we play this video.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Do you recognise this man?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I think this is Mr. Jovan Tintor, as far as I recall, although --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And Mr. Tintor was a prominent member of the SDS in your municipality, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If we could play the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Anchor: That was -- the barricades were -- let's go back to the barricades for a while. People thought it strange that Joja Tintor, who was always there in the leadership of the SDS, mostly seen as -- at press conferences, most of the journalists knew who you were, but then again some people who came from the side didn't know who that man was sitting at the corner of the table. Barricades were set up and you were not in the Holiday Inn. "Jovan Tintor: Well, you see, when the barricades began, I was in Sarajevo, but only once did I succeed in coming to town because I was in the headquarters and involved the organisation, at the top of the organisation for the barricades. Once I went to Vogosca, I went to organise the same thing there. I came back once to Sarajevo and made arrangements with Mr. Dukic but that was mostly by phone of course because -- "Anchor: And the telephone was being tapped? "Jovan Tintor: I know that only too well. They made a good use of it. However, I came back again, went towards the city again. Of course I had good security because I know that Muslims were well armed. At Kobilja Glava there were barricades and I could not go past them to Sarajevo. I tried going through Rajlovac but the same thing happened there as well. Where they put up the barricades, I could not pass to Sarajevo. I went back to Vogosca and in a certain manner I stayed in touch with the headquarters that was in the hands of Mr. Lukic. I was responsible for that part of Vogosca and Ilijas. I had regular contacts with everybody. I believe that it was brilliantly performed. It was an action of which all organisers, military organisers could envy us."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So, in fact, Mr. Sikiras, according to Mr. Tintor, the barricades that Serbs erected in the Vogosca municipality were organised by him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: If that's what he says, then I don't have that information. I told you that I was literally isolated for two months. I didn't leave the village. I hear this statement for the first time --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: -- I can't say anything. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It's a statement of a third party and we don't admit those, and also the witness has not adopted or confirmed anything about the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Rather than explain the custom --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, it's a little unfair to ask Ms. McKenna to deal with this since this is a matter that was raised in court prior to her arrival. But I think the Court will recall that the distinction made was - and it was made repeatedly and made explicitly by Mr. Robinson - that if these are essentially contemporaneous accounts by -- at or around the time by officials in the position to know and so forth, and this is Mr. Tintor -- I think the nature of this -- this is not a statement taken by law enforcement authorities which was one of the distinctions we made in terms of the statement versus other forms of assertions about what happened. We made the point previously that with respect to persons closely associated with the events in question and with the leadership, they basically amounted to admissions that in an adversarial system would be admissible, something I'm sure Judge Morrison in particular is aware of. I think for all those reasons, this -- these statements by Mr. Tintor fall within the parameters of admissibility that have become part of the practice of this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, have we not dealt with the television interview, in particular interviews with video, a bit differently from the pure third-party statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have in some cases, and I'm -- I'm remembering an interview of a Mr. Stanic in particular that you omitted over our objection. And it's still -- and so that's true. But it's our position that this, number one, that this is not a contemporaneous interview, it's one after the fact, and that, nevertheless, we object to it because when an interview -- a substantive interview of someone making a statement after the fact is admitted, we don't have the chance to ask that witness what they meant or confront that evidence. So it's getting something in through the backdoor where this witness also knows nothing about that, which is a second ground for my objection that maybe even in spite of the practice with Mr. Stanic should be upheld because this witness has absolutely given no information about -- that would warrant admission through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Again, I think I'll be repeating points that were made to the Court earlier, but speaking of backdoor, this is just a backdoor hearsay objection. Hearsay is clearly permissible in this institution and Mr. Robinson's objection tries to ignore that. The original concern about statements was the extent to which they may or may not contravene 92 bis and we tried to carve out appropriate and reasonable and pragmatic parameters that dealt with that. That's why a portion of this previous -- of this interview previously was admitted. It's a reflection of precisely what I described earlier. And for these reasons and others, this should be properly admitted and was -- a portion of it was previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tieger - sorry about that - would you describe it as a contemporaneous statement at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a war-time statement, Mr. President. I think in the context we outlined earlier, that would make it contemporaneous. It's a -- it's done in the -- I mean, no one was ever talking about a statement that was made at the exact moment of the events in question. So in terms of the practice that's been developed, contemporaneous was basically linked to the other issue I described, is there this belated, after-the-war effort to collect information by law enforcement officials and others that makes it much more akin to the kind of information that should properly be in the form of 92 bis. But in -- so interviews that took place in the general context of the war, as events were progressing and as political figures and military figures were trying to make known their position to their constituency so that -- to encourage them or to explain their position to internationals, that was contemporaneous in that context. It was considered as such by the Court previously. And as I say, I believe that's part of the reason, although there are others, why Mr. Stanic's statement and a portion of this interview was previously admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, following up on Judge Baird's question, may we know the date of this statement is one thing that would be useful? And secondly, perhaps Mr. Tieger could address how in the -- in our previous practice a statement like this has been admitted through a witness who could provide no information or comment on the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to follow up briefly on the question Mr. Robinson raised, which I'm grateful for because I think it illustrates another reason for the admissibility, this was in 1994 and it was broadcast by Serb Radio and Television. As we learned earlier in the day, that's a Bosnian Serb governmental arm established by the Bosnian Serb authorities for the purpose of disseminating their views. So the provenance -- the reason these things come in is because their provenance is not at issue in any way, shape, or form; it's something that the organs of RS want to be heard; it would be a terrible anomaly if they were to disseminate this, want their constituency, and indeed the whole world to hear it, and yet this Court couldn't consider it in the totality of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we'll stop here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Please, I have to comment this because this is not true. Authorities never edited this. That was completely independent and it was the only service -- state service like BBC and not propaganda device.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll stop here. It has been the practice of this Trial Chamber that a third-party statement may not be admitted unless its content is commented upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand. And even in case of Stanic with respect to Foca municipality, the then-witness commented on some of the statements Stanic made in the video about the SDS policies in Foca municipality. So I -- the Chamber sees no reason to defer from our past practice. Given that witness didn't confirm anything about Mr. Tintor's interview statement, the Chamber will not receive this interview at this time. Let us proceed. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: At paragraph 9 of your statement you state that you organised guards in the village of Grahoviste from April 1992 until 4th of May, 1992. And at paragraph 13 of your statement you state that you kept guard around the village carrying shot-guns that belonged to hunters and a couple of automatic rifles owned by members of the reserve police. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence that as early as January 1992, arms were being distributed from the JNA barracks at Semizovac to Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Chamber and Mr. Karadzic, that's P2344, paragraph 35.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sikiras, were you aware of this distribution?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to look at a report that is in evidence before the Trial Chamber, that's P979. We may have to switch back from Sanction to e-court. And at page 1 of both the English and the B/C/S of this report, you'll see that it is a report authored by Milutin Kukanjac, who was commander of the JNA 2nd Military District, and it's dated the 20th of March, 1992, and it relates to the assessment of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we could move to page 6 of the English and page 7 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I'd like you to focus on heading 5, volunteer forces in the 2nd Military District zone, and if you would look at subsection (c) of section 5 which defines the -- or describes what volunteers are for the purpose of this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably now we need to show the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And then if you focus on subsection (f) which states that the JNA has distributed 51.900 weapons and the SDS 17.298 weapons to these volunteers. Are you following me, Mr. Sikiras?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we move to page 11 in the English and page 16 in the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't able to see where it says that the -- these weapons were distributed to the volunteers. That's in lines 23 and 24 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go back to the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Subsection (c) states that -- the section deals with volunteer forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, section 5 itself deals with the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Volunteer forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- volunteer forces in the second --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Subsection (c) defines what volunteers are for the purposes of this report, namely, conscripts from -- I'm sorry. "No volunteers are potential conscripts for the regular units of the 2nd army and only a small number are from the TO of Bosnia and Herzegovina; in other words, the volunteer units are not part of the JNA and the TO establishment structure." And then subsection (f) details the numbers of weapons distributed to volunteers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So if we could again move to pages 11 of the English version and page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And we see the total weapons distributed is 69.198. And, Mr. Sikiras, if I can ask you to focus on entry number 5 in that list which states Vogosca municipality, 1500. So this report shows that by 20th of March, 1992, 1500 men who were not part of the JNA or the TO had been armed by either the JNA or the SDS in the Vogosca municipality. Were you aware that by the middle of March 1992, 1500 men in your municipality had been so armed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But you yourself were given a rifle in order to defend your village, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that we were such a small group and that due to that we were not given certain things. Only after the fall of the village and after a platoon had been established at Zuc made up of 20 people from Vogosca we organised ourselves and we managed to get hold of some pieces of infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: So you stated that this unit that you joined was disorganised at first but then subsequently became part of the Vogosca Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I don't know precisely about this part of the unit. In my view, it was not organised because during the 20 days that they spent there while the attack was going on, I don't know if there was something happening. I remember an officer passing through. I don't even remember his name. So every day the shift commander would be replaced by someone else and then the new commander would change the whole team and that happened two or three times until the line fell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna, I take it that you need more time? I see the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Yes, very brief, probably five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then we'll take a break after you conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, Your Honour, I don't mean to misrepresent the time, so just in case I take longer, I think we should probably take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. I would ask to be permitted to raise once again the issue that was raised with -- in connection with the admissibility of the interview and in connection with some quick research I undertook and the nature of the argument that was presented. First of all, just so we're on the same playing field, there was reference made to statements and the meaning of statements within the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, strict meaning and how else it's been applied. It should be clear, I hope, that statements within the jurisprudence of the Tribunal refer to information given with an eye toward giving evidence before the Tribunal or possibly a domestic proceeding, that is, documents made in relation to pending or anticipated legal proceedings involving a dispute as to which some fact in that document may be aimed. And as two examples, I would cite the 7 June 2002 Galic decision and the 1 September 2006 Milutinovic decision. But more to the point, Mr. President, there was an issue that was really at the heart of the discussion that I thought was implicit but upon looking at the transcript I should take some responsibility for not making far more clear, and that's the context in which this arises. So reference was made to the practice that existed and the specific example of the Stanic instance and that -- and then Mr. Robinson asked the rhetorical question of the previous practice of admitting a statement that has been -- where a witness has provided information or commented in particular on that -- on the information in question. And of course what that overlooks is the fact that there are, as we've discussed in other contexts, numerous bases for admission, one of which of course has been contextualisation, another one has been affirmation, but the third one of which, which we identified very clearly and has been the basis for admissibility, acknowledged basis for admissibility, is impeachment and that's what this document goes to, and that's the basis for admissibility here. So it's inapposite to compare it to the Stanic situation, which was the Prosecution eliciting sufficient information from the witness about the document so that it was sufficiently contextualised or commented on. This is a situation where no such comment is required, as the Defence has explicitly acknowledged in other circumstances, because it is impeachment. And I can go to the nature of that impeachment although I think it's very clear to the Court, but if I were to do so, I would ask the witness to take off his headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I heard you out, Mr. Tieger, but are you saying that we should reconsider our decision not to admit that document --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- that interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's a sparing use of an in-court motion for reconsideration, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to ask the witness to excuse himself for the moment. Mr. Pejic [sic], if you could understand us, if you could excuse yourself for the moment for us to have a debate in your absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tieger, would you like to continue, in particular as regards your points of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can certainly ask Ms. McKenna to amplify it since it's her witness, but in essence my -- as I understand the evidence, the witness is proffered to offer evidence that the events of the barricade were spontaneous and the Tintor interview goes to contradict that point, showing just the opposite, that they were organised. That's a fairly clear-cut case of impeachment and the admissibility of the document for that reason, as we've seen repeatedly during the course of the Defence case. Now, again, if Ms. McKenna sees a more nuanced aspect that needs to be amplified, I invite her to do that. But that's the thrust of the issue. Witness comes in and says it happened one way, here's an SDS official saying no, it happened in an organised fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tieger, just for my information, the issue of impeachment wasn't raised during argumentation before lunch, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I -- it's true that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: No, I'm just asking. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was not addressed explicitly, but given the context in which the matter arose -- I mean, that's why I didn't stress that point at the time. I thought that given the context in which it arose it was rather implicit. Now looking at the transcript I realised that it may have been overlooked and thought for that reason it should be re-raised with the Court. So my apologies for not making it more explicit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: That's all right. Thank you very much indeed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And further, the witness did not deny the fact that barricades in Sarajevo or in Vogosca municipality were set up by Serbs. He conceded to that possibility, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may briefly amplify. The witness testimony is that the actions that were taken in his village were spontaneous in response to actions taken by the Bosnian Muslims. In his response to the motion to exclude Mr. Sikiras's evidence, Mr. Karadzic stated that this witness's testimony went to the issue of whether the events were simply part of a civil war or were part of a JCE. Now, it's the Prosecution's contention that evidence that Jovan Tintor and the Serb municipality authorities organised the barricades in the municipality directly contradicts Mr. Karadzic's contention and the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are so many hurdles for this to be admitted. First of all, this is for reconsideration. So you've frequently denied a reconsideration on grounds that there's been no justification for -- no injustice by the Trial Chamber's ruling, and under the very high standard of reconsideration, this argument of Mr. Tieger's made this afternoon doesn't meet that standard. Secondly, if you're talking about impeachment, if you look at the witness's statement, there's nothing in the witness's statement that deals with the spontaneity of the barricades. And Mr. Tintor's comments are not directly impeaching of anything that the witness said because it may very well have been that these barricades were organised in response to what they perceived as Muslim acts or Muslim barricades which would not be inconsistent with the witness's statement. Furthermore, it's a very slippery slope to take a comment by someone else in 1994, two years after the fact, and make it admissible as impeachment to a witness who doesn't know that person, who may have no -- who basically has no connection with those events in the way that he would be expected to know the -- what is -- what he's being impeached on. So, for example, if you can bring any witness for the Prosecution, let's say a UN military observer, and he says: I saw the Serbs doing indiscriminate and disproportionate fire. Then you could confront him with a plethora of statements by everybody from the Bosnian Serb leadership saying: No, I never -- we never fired deliberately or indiscriminately, and those could all be admissible under that theory that it impeaches the UN observer's testimony. So I don't think that this impeachment can be used as a bootstrap to admit things that are not otherwise admissible, and I think that the contradiction has to go directly to what the witness would be expected to know. And when we start varying from that principle, I think it just opens the door to statements coming in with witnesses who basically know nothing about the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may respond or reply briefly on the issue of whether or not this document impeaches the witness's testimony. At page 56 of today's transcript at the -- actually, page 55, line 25, I asked whether the barricades that were set up by Serbs were organised by the Serb municipality authorities. And the witnesses said, and I quote: "I can't say anything precisely, although it may have been possible. As for what I know, people usually organised themselves. Where there were more families of the same ethnicity, people organised themselves to prevent any surprises." So it's clearly the -- the witness is clearly testifying that the -- that the barricades were not organised more broadly but were organised on a family-by-family basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry. I hope it's not seen as double teaming, but just with respect to Mr. Robinson's slippery-slope argument that raises a bogeyman which is clearly not implicated by this particular evidence, the foundation for which was laid by Ms. McKenna and her questions to the witness about Mr. Tintor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will put this issue under advisement and give its ruling tomorrow. Let's continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sikiras, for your kind understanding. Ms. McKenna, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Sikiras, just before our first break you described disorganised units -- a unit with commanders coming and going. In your statement, as clarified by your previous testimony today, you stated that at some point your unit became part of the Vogosca Brigade. Now, yesterday when we spoke you stated that you could not recall what date your unit became formally part of the Vogosca Brigade. Is that still correct, you still can't recall that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because I didn't have that information, but since these 20-odd people were coming there over that period, probably that is what it meant. utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I stop you, Mr. Sikiras. The interpreters have asked you to move a little closer to the microphone so that they can hear you. But on the issue of --

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. Do you recall this announcement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I didn't hear this announcement; however, on the radio, whilst we were at Zuc before the platoon was formed, I heard on the radio - I don't know exactly the formulation - but that the army of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been established and I don't know if it is linked to this particular announcement. But I personally didn't hear this announcement. So as I'm telling you, that was at the end of the so-called territory so we were deprived of certain information.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please have document P1505 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Sikiras, this relates to the specific date on which the Vogosca Brigade was formed. And you'll see that this is an order dated the 22nd of May, 1992, from Sarajevo-Romanija Corps Sipcic on the organisational and formation alterations in the SRK. utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

So, Mr. Sikiras, in fact the Vogosca Brigade was formed on the 22nd of May, 1992, and at the date of its formation its commander was Jovan Tintor; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN SIKIRAS
utterances.text: I have to tell you, while I'm looking at this passage, I don't know about Mr. Tintor but I do remember the name of Mr. Vukota Vukovic who is mentioned here as well. He was the one who passed across the line where we were. I have no information about Tintor being -- I really have no information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sikiras.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.text: We don't have the translation, so if you prefer that we -- he interpret it live or if you're willing to -- given that it's a legend, MFI it and have us provide the translation later, one of those two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
