utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to read the short summary of Mr. Lubura's statement in English. [In English] During the war, Veljko Lubura, an educated and experienced electric engineer, was engaged in compulsory work service at the Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska based in Pale. He kept a post of chief engineer for the distribution of electric energy. Upon reorganisation of the Elektroprivreda Republika Srpska in August 1992 he was appointed director of the Elektroprenos plant in Ilidza, that means electro transmission. According to the agreements reached at Sarajevo airport between representatives of the Elektroprivreda Republika Srpska and representatives of the Elektroprivreda BH, the line from Reljevo towards Buca Potok in the Muslim part of Sarajevo was to be used to supply electric power for the needs of the core of city under Muslim control, Grbavica settlement, Hadzici, Ilidza, Rajlovac, Ilijas, and Vogosca, as well as the water-pump station in Bacevo at Ilidza. In 1992 and later on, Serb company led by Mr. Lubura tried to repair the Reljevo-Vogosca and Vogosca-Velesici and Vogosca-Sokolac transmission lines, but mainly failed to do so because of the combat operations and obstruction by the Muslim side. In particular, the Muslim side obstructed the supply of the Vogosca substation where the Pretis and TAS factories were situated. Due to these obstructions, the Velesici substation did not receive electric power to transmit it further across the part of the city under Muslim control. In late 1992, the Serbs managed to put in operation the Visegrad-Rogatica-Sokolac transmission line that the Muslim army had damaged in Gornja Lijeska village and created conditions -- the Serbs created conditions for the hydro power to start operating with technological minimum. The Visegrad-Rogatica-Sokolac-Vogosca transmission line was out of function between Sokolac and Vogosca because it was demolished by Muslim forces in order to prevent the supply to the Pretis and TAS factories in Vogosca. This resulted in the Serbian side being prevented from distributing electric power from Vogosca to Reljevo, Serbian territory, and from Vogosca to Velesici, Muslim territory. In December 1992, the Serbs tried to distribute electric power to Muslim settlement Hrasnica. Given that the Hrasnica-Blazuj transmission line and cables were cut, they were not able to do this without major repair work and these were all along the lines of disengagement between the Serbian and Muslim armies. They were advised to transmit by overhead conductors to the water-supply system in Igman or else Juka Prazina's unit would shell the Serbian area. So the Serbs managed to do this but the voltage from the transmission line to the substation on Hrasnica could not be transmitted due to the failures of this line that was not under Serbian control. This resulted in Blazuj substation being shelled by Juka Prazina units, and for this reason, the whole area of north-western Sarajevo, both Serbian and Muslim parts, remained without electric power supply until the end of January 1993 when the Serbs managed to repair the Blazuj substation. The lack of electric power supply in the core city under the Muslim control was due to the failures in the transmission line which usually occurred along the line of disengagement. When such a thing happened, they would negotiate at the airport to carry out joint repair work in the presence of UNPROFOR. On one occasion, while attempting to repair a transmission line, they came under fire originating from Ugarsko which was under Muslim control. It was only with the liberation of Trnovo in July 1993 that they managed to repair the Buk Bijela-Lukavica transmission line and thus bring in quality energy power from Montenegro to the Lukavica substation for the first time since the beginning of the war. The company of Mr. Lubura also prepared -- were prepared to transmit further part of the energy to substations in Dobrinja, Otoka, and Skenderija on the Muslim side under the condition that the transmission lines connecting these substations were repaired. However, the Muslim side showed no interest in this proposal. Veljko Lubura responsibly claims that nobody, both from the municipal or republican level, civilian or military authorities, ever ordered him, orally or in writing, to cut off electric power supply to any part of Sarajevo and he would not done this even if given such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now this is what I would like us to do, I'd like us to deal with these maps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we have 1D6804, D2541 is its number now, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has been admitted yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was only the statement that was admitted, then? So 1D6804.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, did you mark anything on this map and can you explain to us what this map shows and can you tell us what the notes, or rather, the legend say?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: This is the situation -- this is the situation regarding the transmission lines and transformer stations before the war. The red line are 400-kilowatt transmission lines that came to Reljevo. So the Reljevo transmission station was in this ring of 400-kilowatt lines called Nikola Tesla. They got energy from Mostar and further down there is a transformer station called Cula --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, that is what is written there.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, Mostar-Sarajevo, the 400-kilowatt transmission line. Then Sarajevo 10, Reljevo-Tuzla, is the other transmission line. Then also there is another 400-kilowatt transmission line, Sarajevo 10, Sarajevo 20, Lukavica. So energy could arrive in Reljevo from all sources in Bosnia-Herzegovina and all sources in the former Yugoslavia. Now the black line are 110-kilowatt transmission lines and the dotted black line are the two-system transmission lines. From Reljevo, transformer stations 110, 8, 7, 2, and 5 received their energy, Kosevo, Velesici, Buca Potok, and Azici, so that is the inner city of Sarajevo. From Lukavica it was transformer stations 13, 14, and 15, that's Skenderija, Otoka, and Dobrinja. The transformer station Sarajevo 1, which was built a long time ago, in 1954, received energy from two transmission lines from the Jablanica hydroelectric power-plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, to make it clear to the Trial Chamber, Jablanica is near Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is the first big hydroelectric power-plant that was built after the Second World War, in 1954, and then there was Sarajevo 1 and Sarajevo 2. They were concrete pillars and they are to this day. When the war started, most of these transmission lines had been destroyed because of the war operations. From Reljevo, or rather, from Sarajevo 10 via the 110-kilowatt transmission line, Kiseljak, or rather, the transformer station of Kiseljak received electricity as well. So during the war operations, all the transmission lines were seriously damaged. So the only possibility for Sarajevo to get electric energy from the coal-fired power-plant in Kakanj and from Jablanica was Sarajevo 10, Kiseljak, that transmission line which was linked to 220, that transmission line -- oh, I'm sorry, I'm speaking too fast. So the transmission line Sarajevo 10, Kiseljak was linked up via antennae to the 220-transmission line to Kakanj-Jablanica, and this happened at Kokoska, near Kiseljak. Electric energy was sent via this transmission line to Sarajevo 10, Reljevo, and from there we sent 20 plus 3 megawatt to the transformer station Sarajevo 7, Buca Potok, that was under Muslim control. Also, from Sarajevo 10, 110-kilowatt transmission lines, we followed 20 plus 3 megawatt to the transformer station Sarajevo 1, Blazuj; and 3 megawatt in accordance with our agreement we sent via 10-kilowatt cable to the road network in Bacevo and Konaci.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have all of that in your statement. I wanted to ask you to help the Trial Chamber in the following. Where does this middle transmission line bring electricity from?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Both the Kakanj power-plant and the Jablanica power-plant were under Muslim control. The entire transmission line of Jablanica-Kakanj was under Muslim control as well, and what was our under control was the transmission line up to the separation line with the Croats. And that is Kobiljaca, I think that's the name, to Kobiljaca. So that was under our control. The Buca Potok, Sarajevo 10, transmission line was under our control to -- for a very small section and already further on --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what these three dots on the legend mean?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: The red line [In English] Red line, 400 kV transmission line. [Interpretation] Yes. The black line [In English] Black line, 110 kV TL, yeah, transmission line. [Interpretation] And this black line with these dots, that is two times 110-kilowatt transmission lines. So it's a double system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your previous answer it was not recorded that line 10 was partly under our control, a small part. And then further on and it -- there's no end to that --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Sarajevo 10 -- 7, Buca Potok. Most of the transmission line was under Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this southern and south-eastern part towards Bijela, where did electricity come from there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Electricity came to Lukavica -- before the war came from Reljevo along a 400-kilowatt transmission line and from the hydroelectric power-plant of Mratinje, that is in Montenegro, because the first 400-kilowatt transmission line in Bosnia-Herzegovina was Sarajevo-Buk Bijela. However, to this day its voltage is 220 kV and in Buk Bijela it comes together with the Mratinje-Buk Bijela transmission line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, can this map be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6804 receives number D2542, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one question. Since the confrontation line is not marked here, under whose control were stations 13, 14, 15, Skenderija, Otoka, and Dobrinja, under whose control were these neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Under Muslim control. And, for example, this transmission line, 2 times 110, Sarajevo 20, Lukavica-Skenderija, to this day it hasn't been repaired. The ones towards Dobrinja and Otoka have been repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D6805.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you mark this map? Can you tell us first what the legend says?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: This is the way it is. This is a map of the former JUGEL, that was the former community of power manufacturers of the former Yugoslavia, and it shows all the transmission lines. So the red line, 400 kV transmission line; green line, 220 kV transmission lines; black line, 110 kV transmission lines, along with their respective transformer stations. This is the situation towards the end of 1990. It hasn't changed much to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And during the war - you described this in your statement - you managed to include Visegrad in this network for the Sarajevo zone.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I'll explain this to you. The Visegrad hydroelectric power-plant of 315 megawatt was linked into the electric energy system of the former Yugoslavia with a 400-kilowatt transmission line, Visegrad-Zvornik-Tuzla-Ljubace, but also there were 110 kV transmission lines, Visegrad-Rogatica, transformer station Rogatica, transformer station Sokolac, and transformer station Sarajevo, Vogosca, 4. Also there were two transmission lines, one of them went to Rudo. It operated under 35 but it was designed as a 110 kV transmission line, and then there was the one in Visegrad, going from Visegrad to Gorazde 2 and then Kopaci. In my statement I said Visegrad because the transmission line goes from Visegrad via Zepa, next to Srebrenica, Konjevic Polje, Cerska. It arrives in Begluk Polje, near Zvornik, and from there it leads to Tuzla and Ljubace. It was seriously damaged so the only thing -- so that this Visegrad could function at a technological minimum, at least one generator, we had to repair this 110 kV transmission line to Rogatica and Sokolac and to Hresa, where we linked up. There was actually a bypass and we actually supplied the transformer station at Pale which before the war received electricity from Velesici, that is to say, Sarajevo 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what happens when there are no transmission lines left.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: When there are no transmission lines left, then an exchange has to be switched off. This is a technical question. So the exchange has to be -- has to be switched off, it has -- so the power-plant has to be switched off. There has to be a balance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6805 receives number D2543, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D8618, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, you do understand English?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter that a member of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic, Professor Plavsic, sent to General Morillon. Since you speak English, can you tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic authorised us to negotiate with the Muslim side at the Sarajevo airport. I can just tell you that this man, Spasoje Marinkovic, was an assistant of mine. Dragan Despotovic was director before I became director of transmission. As agreed with me, he went to UNPROFOR and he acted as our liaison person. And these are other staff members of mine, Velimir Radovic, Bratic, Golubovic, Vanovac, so we were in charge of electricity. These were people who worked for me. As for the people down here who were in charge of water, I mean I don't even know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many electric fitters did you have?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: In transmission we covered ten transformer stations and long transmission lines. In order to service this properly and to maintain it properly, even in peace time, I had just one transmission line team, four fitters, and a foreman, and I was supposed to have at least five teams in peace time. The other field was the other service for protection and for measurements. I had four electric fitters, and although I was manager of the plant, I often worked on these actual fittings. So practically most of the time I spent in the car going from one transformer station to another, from Visegrad, Foca, Rudo, in the Sarajevo region, those transformer stations there. You know that, for example, from Ilidza to the transformer station of Lukavica, instead of taking a 10-kilometre road, I went through the woods and took a route of 96 kilometres. So I would spend the entire day to go to repair the equipment at the transformer station of Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just please repeat how long were the transmission lines that were under your authority.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I believe it was over 200 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These teams, did they co-operate with UNPROFOR and did they go out to do repair work and did anyone from your side sabotage this repair work?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Whenever there was a breakage on a transmission line, in particular on these two lines that were supplying both the Serbs and the Muslims, if there was a break we would meet with UNPROFOR at the airport and with UNPROFOR's assistance they would agree with the military commands the date and the time when the repair works would be done. And after that, the Serb and the Muslim teams would go out and carry out the repair work. And that usually happened along the separation line or in the proximity of the separation line. These were the so-called physical repairs and they would sometimes take seven to eight days. The system worked as a one-direction supply. If there is a breakage due to overload, if there is any breakage of devices, these were the situations that could have been rectified more quickly. However, when we had physical damage, that required much more time. First we had to agree on the date and time for repair and UNPROFOR would liaise between the two sides and even sometimes between three sides because sometimes the Croats were involved as well and they had to seek permission. So it took time. Even if the damage was not substantial, it would take five, six, and sometimes even eight days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, could the witness be asked to focus on answering the question. I've refrained until now to raise it, but he's going a lot further than the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So I'll put brief questions and I would ask for brief answers. What was the situation with spare parts during the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: We didn't have enough spare parts, particularly transformer oil, insulators, switches, distribution devices, and protection devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8618 receives number D2544, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly look at 1D8622.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that you are reporting the Executive Committee of Vogosca in this letter?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The 110 power transmission Sokolac-Vogosca was not repaired and we were forced to connect to this transmission line by means of an antenna to 35 kV Pale-Mokro transmission line to build a 35 kV transmission line leading from the village of Poljine and to install a transformer 35 to 10 kV and 8 megawatt amperes and in that way we would secure a proper supply of Vogosca and Ilijas with electric power that was coming from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8622 receives number D2545, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please have 1D8623.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Chamber what this letter of yours means.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Well, look, this is from the statute of Elektroprenos and Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska. Therefore, I had to appoint civilian protection commissioners, and the same situation prevailed in line with the laws that were in force at the time. Each station had a commissioner and below that you can see what their tasks were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show these tasks in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All of this is based on Article 36 of the Law on National Defence.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and it's in accordance with the statute of Elektroprivreda of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8623 receives number D2546, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have 1D8624. I just have to apologise for the fact that a wrong English translation is attached to this document. 1D8624.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what does this pertain to, this document, basically?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: This is the minutes of the meeting held at the Sarajevo airport. I see the name of Jacques Perreaux, the French lieutenant-colonel, the BH delegation, and our delegation, and we were discussing the repair works on transmission lines in order to provide as much energy from Kakanj to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says that the repair work on the Kakanj-Vogosca transmission line had been cancelled due to military problems. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Probably we were not given approval by both armies to proceed with the repair work because basically all the breakages happen along the separation lines, which required both sides to provide and give approvals, because all these repair teams were a mix. They were made up of both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interpreters were not able to hear your question because you were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I'm in a hurry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who is this person in the Serbian delegation under number 1, what was his position?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Bosco Lemez was a member of the Assembly of the city of Sarajevo. He was an electrical engineer. We studied together. And on behalf of the Assembly of the Serbian Sarajevo, he was in charge of utility companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you assess the Serbian delegation in terms of its composition?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Dusko Mijatovic was the technical director of Elektroprenos with a head office in Banja Luka. Dobro Kovacevic was the director of electrical distribution company that held the Sarajevo, Romanija, and Drina region, covering the area with 35, 10 kV and other low-voltage supplies. Dragan Kalajdzija used to work for the ministry for energy at Pale. And Vidoje Magazin was a colonel and this was the only meeting that he attended. He never appeared again later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted temporarily as an MFI'd document, pending the proper translation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D8624 receives number D2547, MFI'd, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lubura, as you have noted, most part of your evidence was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony and now you will be cross-examined by a representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Lubura, I'd like you to look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we could have 65 ter number 2451 -- 24251, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We saw a moment ago the large map, P2542; however, it's quite illegible so I would just like you to look at the map that's coming up on the screen and tell me if this was how the electrical -- the electricity grid was working in -- during the conflict, 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could just enlarge it, please. And again.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, we can see here that this is an OSCE map prepared in 2010, but would you agree that this is the same grid that was working during the conflict with the exception of the Bosanski Petrovac-Kljuc transmission line?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: It's the same map as the one that I provided. There's no difference. 400 kV, 220 kV, 110 kV, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And we can see from Visegrad the green line going east into Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And we can also -- sorry, and then we can also see the green line going down from Foca, just below Foca, going into Montenegro, and that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I'm going to explain this to you. The red line that passes by Foca is Lukavica-Buk Bijela transmission line and it is connected with Montenegro. It was built before the war. However, the one leading from Visegrad to Uzicka Pozega was constructed in the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I tender that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24251 receives number P6035, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: To assist the Chamber in following your evidence, I think if we look at the zoomed-in map which you provided, which is P2542 -- D2542. Now, Mr. Lubura, in 1992, once the confrontation lines were drawn, the substations under BH control were the following, and I think that you've said this already this morning -- this afternoon: Sarajevo 7, which is Buca Potok; Sarajevo 2, which is Veselici; Sarajevo 5, which is Kosevo; Sarajevo 13, which is Skenderija; Sarajevo 14, Otoka; Sarajevo 15, Dobrinja; and Sarajevo 18, Hrasnica or, as is noted on this map, Famos?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, Hrasnica Famos.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And under the control of the Bosnian Serbs were Sarajevo 10 being Reljevo?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Reljevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sarajevo 4 being Vogosca; Sarajevo 8 being Azici; and Sarajevo 20 being Lukavica; and Sarajevo 1 being Blazuj. That's right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Azici were belonging to the Muslim side. That's Azici, Sarajevo 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ah, thank you for that clarification. In order for electricity to get to the substations within the city of Sarajevo under Bosnian control, it necessarily had to pass through either Sarajevo 1, 4, 20, or 10; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So electricity had to pass through the Bosnian Serb-controlled substations to get to the city? You're nodding. You need to put an affirmative answer on the record "yes."

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: That is correct. Electrical power could be distributed to BH-controlled or Muslim-controlled substations from Sarajevo 10 or Sarajevo 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Or 1 or 4?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: It -- yes, it was possible, from 4, that is, Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also number 1, Blazuj?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Only as far as Famos, two times 110.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And if there had been a Bosnian Serb political desire to deny or limit to any -- limit service to any substations in the Muslim-controlled area of Sarajevo, this could have been accomplished?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this. We received --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But Mr. -- sorry, Mr. Lubura --

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: -- electrical power from Muslim sources --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: May I -- that question I think requires a "yes" or a "no" answer. If there'd been a desire, it could have been accomplished? It was technically possible, yes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: It's possible, of course it's quite possible. But also, they would immediately disconnect us from the source. So neither of us would have any electricity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to discuss now some -- I want to move on now to just talk a little bit about your responsibilities. So as director of the Elektroprenos plant in Ilidza, your responsibilities included the administration and maintenance of the Serb-controlled substations and transmission lines in the Sarajevo area; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, under Serb control. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You commenced this role starting in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when repairs were needed, it was your company that sent the technicians to carry out the work?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And as you said a short while ago, that -- sometimes alongside UNPROFOR and technicians from the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Repairs were mostly carried out together, at the separation lines, where most of the damage was on the transmission lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And I think you said earlier that if there were areas that were unsafe, such as ongoing fighting, the military or the police forces could prevent the technicians from entering the area?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I didn't have any problems at the transmission lines that were under Serb control, I had no problems either with the military or the police. We regularly maintained this and repaired it. However, at the separation line, we had to receive the consent of both the Serb and the Muslim side in order to carry out repairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you said earlier, I think at page 91, that you had to get approval by the armies required before repairs could be taken out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: Correct, and that's what UNPROFOR would do. The representatives of UNPROFOR would get the approval both of the Serb army and the Muslim army, and then we would go out into the field together and repair the transmission lines together.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the Bosnian Serb side did deny access to repair lines, did they not?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO LUBURA
utterances.text: I personally do not know about that. That was a matter for UNPROFOR. They were the ones who were in charge of this operation and then they would inform us that they had received approval and that we could go out and repair what was to be repaired. That was the duty of UNPROFOR and that was what we had agreed upon at Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also get a time-frame for this? When was it that the Serb army denied this and for what reason?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time and I -- Mr. Reid informs me we're sitting until 14.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll continue tomorrow. Mr. Lubura, we'll continue tomorrow. There's one matter I'd like to deal with in your absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
